About the Noh Play "Surigami"

In the Sendai Domain, where Noh theater flourished, several new Noh plays were created during the Edo period, and "Surigami" is one such work. The author was Hiraga Kurando Yoshimasa, a retainer of the Sendai Domain, who is said to have presented the text to Date Shigemura. The premiere took place several generations later, during the reign of Date Saimune. Because it drew upon the deeds of the domain's founder, there were reportedly strict restrictions on its performance; however, since the Date family of Iwadeyama preserved it within the Shunfuji school and made it a tradition to chant it during the New Year, it seems to have been reasonably well-known. (※Shunfuji school: One of the schools of Noh waki roles. The founder is said to be Shunfuji Rokuro Jiro, though other theories exist. It flourished as the affiliated school of the Konparu troupe, but declined after the Meiji era and was abolished in 1945 (Showa 20). by Yahoo! Dictionary) The author, Hiraga Kurando Yoshimasa, is believed to be the Hiraga Izumo Yoshimasa mentioned in the entry for the Hiraga clan in the "Private Biographical Dictionary of Sendai Domain Retainers." The Hiraga clan was a lineage ranked among the seated retainers with a stipend of 100 kanmon; since they served the Date family since the time of Date Naomune and resided at the Uchibaba Yamaguchi residence, they called themselves the Baba clan until the Enpo era.

The Noh play takes the form of a "katsu-shura mugen-no" (victory-shura dream-vision play), recounting the Battle of Surigami Ue with Munemi as the shite.

(First Act) While returning to Kyoto after participating in the Date clan's annual New Year's Seven-Herb Renga, the Hogen (of the Inawashiro clan) decides to visit Kodaira-gata Tenmangu Shrine in Inawashiro, a place tied to his ancestors. Upon arriving in Inawashiro and gazing at Kurokawa Castle from afar, he recalls Masamune's poem—"Picking the seven herbs, all gathered on a single leaf"—which served as the origin of the Seven-Herb Renga. Just then, an old man appears from nowhere and asks him about the spirit of the poem. When the Hogen replies, "You mean the seven herbs of spring," the old man explains, "That is true, but it is a poem in which Lord Komon (Masamune) subdued enemies from seven different places." The Hogen asks the old man for directions to Kodaira-gata Tenmangu Shrine; guided by him, he arrives safely at the shrine, where the plum blossoms are in full bloom. As they enjoy the blossoms together, the old man points out famous sites along the Way of the Immortals. Eventually, evening falls. When he requests music so they can enjoy the night together, the old man vanishes, blending into the evening mist. (Intermission) (Second Act) As the Hogen plays music just as the old man wished, a splendid warrior appears in the moonlight and identifies himself as Shigezane Date. Shigezane recounts the events of the Battle of Surigami Ue and celebrates the glory of the Sendai Domain.

Admin's Thoughts

It's quite something how he managed to produce a piece of historical fiction about the domain founder in that era (lol). The author must have been someone who absolutely loved writing this kind of thing. It somehow makes sense that this was written by an amateur rather than a professional. Perhaps they felt hesitant to make Masamune the protagonist, or maybe they were selected because they had written the "Shigezane-ki"—either way, the protagonist is Shigezane. However, based on the text, there is absolutely no necessity for Shigezane to be the protagonist. I feel they introduced a bit too many characters and leaned too heavily into the narrative. It wouldn't be strange for any of the military commanders mentioned in the text to be the protagonist. If they wanted to glorify Masamune, I think it would have turned out cleaner if Masamune had been the protagonist, but I suppose they were just hesitant. Since Shigezane was the key figure who passed down Masamune's story to later generations, I think he was a suitable second-best choice. But because they chose Shigezane, the text of the second act probably drifted toward a "narrative" style... If they had done this (the content of the second act) via interspersed narration, and then ended the second act with text more suited for a captivating kakeri... (← I'm being too greedy!)

The procession and descriptions of famous sites in the first act feature a parade of Mutsu's utamakura, designed so that you can enjoy a trip without even leaving your seat. For Mutsu's utamakura, please refer to this site “Ezo, Mutsu, Utamakura”. I've also included links within the main text.

The famous sites of the Sendo aren't visible from the Aizu Basin, but let's just say it would be tactless to point that out. After all, it explicitly says "crossing the mountains." I wonder if it would be wrong to meet the old man in Inawashiro, rather than on the Sendo, and then have him point out the sights as they travel... (I'm really nitpicking here (＾＾A)). Also, some might point out that since one person cannot play both the drum and the flute simultaneously, a waki-tsure should be brought in; however, since it's rare for waki-tsure to have their own lines, there may have been a proper attendant monk during the performance.

In typical productions, the later shite is a young warrior. And if there's a kogaki where they perform as an old warrior, it really gets me.

Bonus

By the way, Katsu-shura plays are extremely rare; among the current repertoire, there are "Ebisu" and "Tamura."

"Yashima"

only the third act. Among the Taiko No plays still performed today, the Katsu-shura is only the first act, "Akechi-uchi." See:

Nohgaku Land

Nohgaku Association

Among these, "

Yashima

」is renowned as a masterpiece, but the administrator absolutely loves the closing lines. From the gripping depiction of the naval battle, the mood shifts abruptly to "What appeared to be the enemy were flocks of seagulls..."—a satisfying conclusion befitting its dreamlike reputation.

It's quite something how he managed to produce a piece of historical fiction about the domain founder in that era (lol).
